'''Tebello Nyokong''' {{post-nominals|commas=on|country=ZAR|OMB|FRS|HonFRSC|FRSSAf}} (born 20 October 1951) is a South African [[chemist]] and distinguished professor at [[Rhodes University]].

She is currently researching [[Photodynamic therapy|photo-dynamic therapy]], an alternative cancer treatment method to [[chemotherapy]].<ref name=ForbesAfria2015/><ref name="AAS">{{cite web |title=Nyokong Tebello {{!}} The AAS |url=https://www.aasciences.africa/fellow/nyokong-tebello |website=The African Academy of Sciences |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211005232830/https://www.aasciences.africa/fellow/nyokong-tebello |archive-date=October 5, 2021}}</ref> In 2007, she was one of the top three publishing scientists in South Africa. 

==Early life and education==
{{Quote box
 | quote  ="You believe you can be a wife and a mother and still be a bread winner and contribute to society. And you will" – Tebello Nyokong<ref name=sourceok>{{cite web |url=https://scienceclubforgirls.wordpress.com/2011/03/08/tebello-nyokongs-letter-to-her-young-self/ |title=Tebello Nyokong's Letter to her 18-year-old Self |author=Tebello Nyokong |date=8 March 2011 |website=scienceclubforgirls.wordpress.com |access-date=9 November 2015 }}</ref>
 | width  =25%
 | align  =left
}}

Tebello Nyokong was born in [[Maseru]], Lesotho on 20 October 1951 but spent most of her youth in South Africa.<ref name=bibliography>[https://www.gov.za/about-government/tebello-nyokong-1951#:~:text=Tebello%20Nyokong%20was%20born%20in,anything%20a%20boy%20could%20do Tebello Nyokong - South African Government], Retrieved 9 May 2024</ref>

Nyokong came from a poor background facing challenging circumstances. After being sent to live with her grandparents in the mountains of Lesotho she partitioned her childhood caring for sheep and going to school. Nyokong says that she would spend one day at school and then one day with the sheep as someone had to care for them.<ref name=seasvid>[http://21icons.com/seasons/ Video interview with Tebello Nyokong], 21 icons, Retrieved 9 November 2015</ref> She published an open letter that she wrote nominally aimed at her 18-year-old self.<ref name=nature>{{cite web |url=http://blogs.nature.com/soapboxscience/2014/10/13/distinguished-south-african-professor-tebello-nyokong-on-science-education-and-innovation |title=Distinguished South African Professor Tebello Nyokong on science, education and innovation |last=Jackson |first=Alex |date=13 October 2014 |website=Nature.com blogs |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190126221313/http://blogs.nature.com/soapboxscience/2014/10/13/distinguished-south-african-professor-tebello-nyokong-on-science-education-and-innovation |archive-date=26 January 2019 }}</ref> It reflected that despite the hardships she would face her hard work would allow her to excel in mathematics and science, proving that material poverty does not equate to intellectual poverty. She reminded her self to trust her independent mind and not be swayed by peers or societal expectations and that her determination and love for science would guide her to not only a fulfilling career but also a family and that she would contribute to society.<ref name=sourceok/>

Two years before her [[Matriculation in South Africa|matric year]] she changed from art studies to the sciences, developing an interest in chemistry. She received her Cambridge Overseas School Certificate in 1972.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Sefala |first1=Ntshephe |title=The Presidency Republic of South Africa |url=http://www.thepresidency.gov.za/national-orders/recipient/tebello-nyokong-1951 |archive-date=10 May 2019 |access-date=30 October 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190510090551/http://www.thepresidency.gov.za/national-orders/recipient/tebello-nyokong-1951 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Nyokong obtained her bachelor's degree in both chemistry and biology from the [[National University of Lesotho]] in 1977 followed by a Master's degree in Chemistry in 1981 from [[McMaster University]] in [[Ontario, Canada]]. In 1987, she received her Ph.D. in chemistry from the [[University of Western Ontario]].<ref name=Rhodes>{{cite web|title=Prof Tebello Nyokong|url=https://www.ru.ac.za/nanotechnology/staff/profnyokong/|website=Rhodes University|date=17 April 2012 |accessdate=9 November 2015}}</ref> After earning her PhD, she received a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright fellowship]] to continue her post-doctoral studies at the [[University of Notre Dame]] in the United States.

==Career==
{{Scholia}}
After finishing her Fulbright fellowship in the United States, Nyokong briefly returned to Lesotho to take a position at the University of Lesotho before taking a position as a lecturer at Rhodes University in 1992.<ref name=AAS/> The National Research Foundation gave her a high rating and helped Nyokong obtain a research laboratory at the university.<ref name=Presidency/> Soon, she moved from lecturer to professor, and then distinguished professor.<ref name=Presidency/> She is known for her research in [[nanotechnology]], as well as her work on photo-dynamic therapy.  Her pioneering research in the latter is paving the way for a safer cancer detection and treatment, without the debilitating side effects of chemotherapy.<ref name=AAS/>

Nyokong’s research group is involved in the development of multifunctional nanodrugs for diagnostics and therapy by chemically linking [[metal|metallic]], [[magnetism|magnetic]], or [[semiconductor]] [[nanoparticle]]s to [[photochemistry|photoactive]] [[phthalocyanine]] photosensitizers.<ref name=Nyokong2013>{{cite journal |url=https://pubs.aip.org/aip/acp/article/1517/1/49/816683/The-use-of-phthalocyanines-in-cancer-therapy |title=The use of phthalocyanines in cancer therapy |last1=Nyokong |first1=Tebello |last2= Gledhill |first2=Igle |journal=AIP Conf. Proc. |volume=1517 |pages=49–52 |year=2013 |issue=1 |doi=10.1063/1.4794220 |bibcode=2013AIPC.1517...49N |url-access=subscription }}</ref> These nanoparticles are designed to accumulate at target sites due to the [[enhanced permeability and retention effect|enhanced permeability and retention (EPR) effect]]. Nanoparticles can be modified with various [[functional group]]s to act as [[photosensitizer]]s or carriers, creating an all-in-one therapeutic tool. This tool can absorb a broad spectrum of light and convert it to [[phototoxicity|phototoxic]] species within [[neoplasm|tumor cells]], leading to targeted destruction requiring low light intensity and drug doses.<ref name=Nyokong2013/> Nyokong noted an exciting scientific challenge facing her field was developing better hybrid materials that act as photocatalysts, which could offer therapeutic value and resistance to microorganisms while also not acting as pollutants.<ref>{{cite journal |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-019-0236-7 |title=Charting a course for chemistry |journal=[[Nature Chemistry]] |volume=11 |date=April 2019 |page=290 |doi=10.1038/s41557-019-0236-7 |last1=Aspuru-Guzik |first1=Alán |last2=Baik |first2=Mu-Hyun |last3=Balasubramanian |first3=Shankar |last4=Banerjee |first4=Rahul |last5=Bart |first5=Suzanne |last6=Borduas-Dedekind |first6=Nadine |last7=Chang |first7=Sukbok |last8=Chen |first8=Peng |last9=Corminboeuf |first9=Clemence |last10=Coudert |first10=François-Xavier |last11=Cronin |first11=Leroy |last12=Crudden |first12=Cathleen |last13=Cuk |first13=Tanja |last14=Doyle |first14=Abigail G. |last15=Fan |first15=Chunhai |last16=Feng |first16=Xinliang |last17=Freedman |first17=Danna |last18=Furukawa |first18=Shuhei |last19=Ghosh |first19=Suhrit |last20=Glorius |first20=Frank |last21=Jeffries-El |first21=Malika |last22=Katsonis |first22=Nathalie |last23=Li |first23=Ang |last24=Linse |first24=Sara Snogerup |last25=Marchesan |first25=Silvia |last26=Maulide |first26=Nuno |last27=Milo |first27=Anat |last28=Narayan |first28=Alison R. H. |last29=Naumov |first29=Panče |last30=Nevado |first30=Cristina |issue=4 |pmid=30903035 |bibcode=2019NatCh..11..286A |display-authors=1 }}</ref>

In 2014 she was a professor at [[Rhodes University]] in [[Grahamstown]]. She was the subject for a photographic portrait for [[Adrian Steirn]]'s ''21 icons''<ref name=season2>[http://21icons.com/seasons/ Promise of Freedom], 21 icons, Retrieved 9 November 2015</ref> which imagined her returned to her childhood role as a [[shepherd]] but now the shepherd is an adult and she is wearing her chemist's white coat. Copies of the picture were sold for charity.<ref name=news>[http://www.news24.com/Archives/City-Press/Behind-the-Icon-Tebello-Nyokong-The-compassionate-scientist-20150429 Behind the Icon – Tebello Nyokong: The compassionate scientist], 10 May 2014, News24, Retrieved 9 November 2015</ref>

In 2021, Nyokong co-wrote an article in [[Nature Materials]] highlighting obstacles facing researchers in Africa.<ref name=NatMat2021>{{cite journal |url=https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-021-00961-0 |title=Overcoming hurdles facing researchers in Africa |last1=Nyokong |first1=Tebello |last2=Ngoy |first2=Bokolombe P. |last3=Amuhaya |first3=Edith K. |journal=[[Nature Materials]] |volume=20 |page=570 |year=2021 |issue=4 |doi=10.1038/s41563-021-00961-0 |pmid=33723421 |bibcode=2021NatMa..20..570N |url-access=subscription }}</ref> She and her colleagues wrote that while the government funded university salaries and basic maintenance, international partners were needed to bring more resources to fund research itself. They also noted that collaborative efforts foster a more integrated scientific community and that more effort is needed to bridge the gap between academic research and marketable products, known as the innovation chasm.<ref name=NatMat2021/>

==Awards and recognition==
Nyokong is a recipient of South Africa's [[Order of Mapungubwe]], South Africa's highest honour.<ref name=Presidency>{{cite web|title=Tebello Nyokong|url=http://www.thepresidency.gov.za/pebble.asp?relid=7660|website=The Presidency, Republic of South Africa|accessdate=9 November 2015|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20151121034719/http://www.thepresidency.gov.za/pebble.asp?relid=7660|archivedate=21 November 2015}}</ref> She received the [[L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Awards|L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Award]] representing Africa and the Arab States in 2009,<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.fondationloreal.com/our-programs-women-science/laureates-loreal-unesco-women-science-international-award |title=Laureates of the L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science International Award |website=www.fondationloreal.com }}</ref> the South African Chemical Institute Gold Medal in 2012,<ref>{{cite magazine |url=https://www.funtimesmagazine.com/2021/12/31/379676/5-african-scientists-we-need-to-celebrate |title=5 African Scientists We Need to Celebrate |last= Subramanian |first=Anand |date=December 31, 2021 |magazine=Funtimes }}</ref> and was named one of the Top 10 Most Influential Women in Science and Technology in Africa by [[IT News Africa]].<ref name=ForbesAfria2015>{{cite web |url=https://www.forbesafrica.com/woman/2014/06/01/from-shepherd-to-scientist/ |title=From Shepherd To scientist |date=2015 |website=Forbes Africa }}</ref> In 2013 she was awarded the National Research Foundation's Lifetime Achievement Award.<ref name=Rhodes/> In 2016 she received the [[African Union Kwame Nkrumah Award for Scientific Excellence]] at the Continental level in the Basic Science, Technology and Innovation category and in 2017 the Black Science, Technology & Engineering Professionals (BSTEP) Excellence Award.<ref>{{cite web | last=| first=| title=Legendary South African Scientist Wins Excellence Award | website=SA People | date=2017-12-08 | url=https://www.sapeople.com/education/legendary-scientist-inspires-students-excellence/ | access-date=2025-03-26}}</ref>
